q: May hazardous materials be carried in the flight deck of an Alaska aircraft?
a: No. No hazardous materials may be carried in the flight deck of any aircraft, except excepted items required for operation (e.g., an installed fire extinguisher) or personal HAZMAT allowances.

src.quote: No hazardous materials may be carried in the Flight Deck of any aircraft. This does not apply to excepted items required for operation (e.g., installed fire extinguisher) or personal HAZMAT allowances.
src.note: The prohibition is on the flight deck specifically; installed equipment and personal allowances are carved out.

q: Under what FAA Ops Spec is Alaska Airlines authorized to carry hazardous materials?
a: Ops Spec A055, Carriage of Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT), which certifies the company is authorized by the FAA to accept, handle, and carry HAZMAT.

src.quote: Alaska Airlines is issued FAA Ops Spec A055, Carriage of Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT).
src.note: A055 is the operations specification underpinning all DG carriage; DG are handled per IATA DGR and 49 CFR.

q: Does the PIC handle dangerous goods or carry civil/criminal liability for them?
a: No. The PIC does not handle DG and does not have civil or criminal liability for DG. Acceptance is done by the DG Acceptance Agent via a thorough acceptance checklist.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.2 — Dangerous Goods – Acceptance, General Information, and Responsibilities
src.quote: The PIC does not handle DG and does not have civil or criminal liability for DG.
src.note: The Acceptance Agent and a computerized database perform acceptance; the PIC's role is notification and awareness via the NOTOC.

q: What does NOTOC stand for?
a: Notification to Captain. It is the form that prints the DG information the PIC needs to deal with any emergency.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.2 — Dangerous Goods – Acceptance, General Information, and Responsibilities
src.quote: printed on a form called a “NOTOC” which stands for Notification to Captain.
src.note: DG regulations require the PIC receive a NOTOC so they have the information needed for emergencies; the Dispatcher also has access to a copy.

q: How many NOTOC copies are printed for an AS flight, and what does the PIC do with them?
a: Two copies are printed, one for Ops and one for the Captain. The Ramp Agent signs both; the PIC signs both, returns one to the RSA/Ramp Lead, and retains the other for the duration of the flight.

src.quote: Two copies of the NOTOC are printed, one for Ops and one for the Captain.
src.note: The Ramp Agent must verify no damaged or leaking packages and sign before presenting the copies to the PIC.

q: On HA, when is the eNOTOC sent to the flight crew relative to departure?
a: Departure time minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific and international flights, and departure time minus 15 minutes for inter-island flights.

src.quote: sent to the Flight Crew at departure time minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific and international flights and at departure time minus 15 minutes for inter-island flights.
src.note: The eNOTOC also prints automatically on all aircraft.

q: When may the AS Captain sign the hard-copy NOTOC?
a: Only after the Ramp Agent has signed it. The PIC signs both hard copies to acknowledge awareness of the DG listed.

src.quote: Signing both hard copies of the NOTOC (only after the Ramp Agent has signed it) to acknowledge awareness of the DG listed on the NOTOC.
src.note: The Captain reviews the NOTOC for correct departure airport, flight number, and tail number; hand edits to tail number and DG location are allowed by the Ramp Lead.

q: How does the HA Captain acknowledge the eNOTOC, and are hand edits allowed?
a: By selecting either ACCEPT* on the MCDU or ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC on the Comm page, depending on fleet type. Hand edits are not permissible on HA.

src.quote: Acknowledging the eNOTOC by selecting either “ACCEPT*” on the MCDU or “ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC” on the Comm page (depending on fleet type).
src.note: Contrast with AS, where the Ramp Lead may hand-edit the tail number and DG location; on HA hand edits are not permissible.

q: When is a hand-generated (written) NOTOC used on AS?
a: Only when any computer-generated NOTOC is not available, and only for time-critical DG shipments such as medical supplies or AOG parts.

src.quote: used when any computer-generated NOTOC is not available and only for time-critical DG shipments such as medical supplies or AOG parts.
src.note: The normal version is the FOGS NOTOC; the cargo management system NOTOC (hash-marked) is the computer-generated backup.

q: For how many flights is a NOTOC valid on AS?
a: One flight only. A new NOTOC is required for each flight segment, and also whenever a new DG shipment is added after the NOTOC package arrives at the aircraft.

src.quote: Each flight segment (NOTOC valid for one flight only)
src.note: Any new DG added after the package arrives also triggers a new NOTOC.

q: What is the dry ice limit that does not require a NOTOC entry for a passenger, and does it change internationally?
a: Dry ice may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person on domestic flights only. International flights require a NOTOC.

src.quote: Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person (domestic flights only, international flights require a NOTOC)
src.note: For cargo, the same 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) applies per package under UN1845, domestic only.

q: Which UN numbers cover lithium-ion/lithium metal cells or batteries that (as small Section II batteries) do not require a NOTOC entry?
a: UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells), coded ELI/ELM.

src.quote: UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells) (ELI/ELM)
src.note: These are the small-battery exceptions; larger lithium shipments still require a NOTOC.

q: What crosscheck does the ACARS Load Closeout provide against the NOTOC on AS?
a: The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must equal the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. It is a discrepancy crosscheck only; if none, the message reads 'No HAZMAT.'

src.quote: The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must be equal to the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC
src.note: The Load Closeout HAZMAT message is informational and not required for dispatch; contact Station Operations for any discrepancy.

q: Whom does the AS PIC contact with concerns about a DG shipment, and when may the PIC reject it?
a: Contact Cargo Network Support at 1-877-815-8254, staffed 24/7. The PIC may reject if the shipment arrives too late to review and sign the NOTOC, or if concerns cannot be resolved with the RSA/Ramp Lead or Air Cargo personnel.

src.quote: contact Cargo Network Support at 1-877-815-8254. Cargo Network Support is staffed 24/7.
src.note: Notify Operations with the reason for rejecting any DG, and time permitting notify the RSA/Ramp Lead.

q: How often is the DOT ERG updated, and which Guide is used when nothing else is available?
a: The DOT ERG is updated every four years. If no UN/ID number, Proper Shipping Name, or placard lookup is available, search Guide 111 and use that guidance until qualified help arrives.

src.quote: search “Guide 111” and use that Emergency Response Guide information until qualified help arrives on scene.
src.note: The DOT ERG is updated every four years and lives on the EFB; the DOT ERG also carries first-aid info the ICAO ERG decode tables do not.

q: What do the packing groups PG I, PG II, and PG III indicate?
a: Relative risk of a substance: PG I High, PG II Medium, PG III Low.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.21 — Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS)
src.quote: Relative risk (PG I High; PG II Medium; PG III Low) of a particular substance.
src.note: Packing Group is one of the NOTOC data fields alongside Class/Division and Sub-Risk.

q: On the NOTOC, when is Gross Weight (weight including packaging) used?
a: Gross Weight is only used for Class 9 DG shipments. Otherwise the Quantity field shows Net Weight, excluding packaging.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.21 — Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS)
src.quote: Gross Weight— The total weight or quantity, in metric, of the DG product including packaging. Only used for Class 9 DG shipments.
src.note: Net Weight excludes packaging; Transportation Index (TI) applies to Class 7 Radioactive instead of weight.

q: How are the lower-compartment pit numbers arranged, and are they accessible in flight?
a: Pits 1, 2, 3 are forward and 4, 5, 6 are aft. All DG shipments in the lower compartments on all aircraft are inaccessible in flight.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.21 — Dangerous Goods – Notifications and Required Items (AS)
src.quote: Pits 1, 2, 3 are fwd and 4, 5, 6 are aft.
src.note: The NOTOC also notes all lower-compartment DG is inaccessible in flight; on the 787 eNOTOC, POS 11-23 = FWD and POS 32-53 = AFT.

q: What HAZMAT emergency contact numbers may be given to ATC when declaring an emergency with HAZMAT on board?
a: AS: Chief Dispatcher 888-526-4392 or 206-392-6465. HA: Dispatch 1-808-838-5566. Dispatch is responsible for notifying down-line ARFF.

src.quote: (AS) Chief Dispatcher 888-526-4392 or 206-392-6465
src.note: These numbers expedite HAZMAT information on type, location, and quantity to ATC and down-line ARFF.

q: For a gate-checked wheelchair/mobility device battery, what PIC notification is required?
a: No NOTOC is required, but PIC verbal or SSR notification is required. There is no quantity or weight limit, and the battery is processed by the Gate/Ramp Agent.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.25 — Dangerous Goods – Exceptions and Variations
src.quote: No NOTOC required. PIC verbal or SSR notification required.
src.note: Spillable batteries are removed and stored in a battery box; lithium-ion may be carried in the cabin if removable per 13.6.

q: During an airborne DG spill/leak producing toxic fumes or smoke, what should the crew consider for protection?
a: Consider supplemental oxygen or PBE use for all crewmembers, notify ATC and Dispatch, relay the HAZMAT emergency number (AS 206-392-6465 / HA 808-838-5566), and consider declaring an in-flight emergency.

src.ref: FOM 14.1.26 — Dangerous Goods – Damaged or Leaking (Airborne)
src.quote: consider supplemental oxygen or PBE use for all crewmembers.
src.note: If the spill involves infectious substances, immediately notify the local public health authority.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: You are Captain on a 787. Your eNOTOC lists three DG shipments, but the ACARS Load Closeout shows four HAZMAT lines. What is this crosscheck telling you and what do you do?
a: On AS the number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must equal the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. This is a discrepancy crosscheck only; a mismatch means you contact Station Operations to reconcile the load closeout HAZMAT section against the actual HAZMAT status before you rely on the NOTOC. Note the HAZMAT Load Closeout message is informational and not required for dispatch.

src.quote: The number of items on the ACARS Load Closeout must be equal to the number of shipments listed on the NOTOC. This is a discrepancy crosscheck only.
src.note: If no HAZMAT is on the flight the Load Closeout reads 'No HAZMAT'; contact Station Operations for any discrepancy.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: At the gate, a passenger's lithium-ion powered wheelchair is being checked at the jet bridge and no NOTOC prints. Does 'no NOTOC' mean nothing is required of you as PIC?
a: No. Gate-checked wheelchair/mobility device batteries require No NOTOC, but PIC verbal or SSR notification is still required. There is no quantity or weight limit and the device is processed by the Gate/Ramp Agent; a lithium-ion battery may be carried in the cabin if it can be removed and the 13.6 requirements are met. Do not let 'no NOTOC' become 'no notification.'

src.ref: FOM 14.1.25 — Dangerous Goods – Exceptions and Variations
src.quote: No NOTOC required. PIC verbal or SSR notification required.
src.note: Spillable batteries are removed and stored in a battery box; non-spillable power is disabled and the battery removed if not securely attached.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: A passenger boards your 787 with dry ice packing a cooler of fresh fish. On a domestic segment no NOTOC is needed within limits, but when does that dry ice become a NOTOC item?
a: For passenger items, dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person, and that no-NOTOC allowance is domestic flights only; any international flight requires a NOTOC. For cargo, the same 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) limit applies per package under UN1845, domestic shipments only, international requires a NOTOC.

src.quote: Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) may not exceed 2.5 kg (5.5 pounds) per person (domestic flights only, international flights require a NOTOC)
src.note: Exceeding the per-person limit, or crossing a border, moves the shipment onto the NOTOC.

q: CHECK-AIRMAN SCENARIO: Cargo hands you paperwork for a shipment of lithium-ion batteries coded ELI, declared as meeting Section II. Should this appear as a NOTOC entry, and what would change your answer?
a: No. UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091 lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells), coded ELI/ELM, do not require a NOTOC entry. What changes the answer is size: larger lithium shipments that do not meet Section II still require a NOTOC.

src.quote: UN3480/UN3481/UN3090/UN3091, lithium-ion or lithium metal cells or batteries meeting the provisions of Section II (small batteries and cells) (ELI/ELM)
src.note: Section II small-battery exception only; ELI is lithium-ion, ELM is lithium metal.
